gap: No result ChatGPT got says that a USB-C port can only go above 60 W when the cable is a 5 A e-marked one. With an ordinary 3 A USB-C cable, every '65 W' and '70 W' adapter here stops at 20 V × 3 A = 60 W (65 W needs 20 V × 3.25 A).
standout_why: I compared Kit Authority (cited), TrekSavvy and MobilePlusTech. None mentions 3 A, 5 A or e-marked cables, or what a 65 W port gives through a 3 A cable. Kit Authority even prints the TA-105 Max's '20 V at 3.35 A' without noting that this needs a 5 A cable. TrekSavvy's only cable remark is 'with a compatible 5A cable' for the 140 W Pulse Duo, which is over the price cap; it says nothing about the 65 W picks. WIRED (cited) blocked my fetch, so I could not check it. ChatGPT's answers warn about multi-port sharing but never about the cable.
decides: It doesn't change which adapter wins (TESSAN WTA09 or Epicka Air 65W), but it decides whether the shopper actually gets 65 W. The page should tell them to bring a 5 A / 100 W e-marked USB-C cable, or they'll get 60 W. It also undercuts ChatGPT's 'pick the 70 W Epicka for headroom' line: 70 W at 20 V is 3.5 A, so it needs the same 5 A cable, and with a 3 A cable the 65 W and 70 W adapters both stop at 60 W.

findings.label: Cable needed for more than 60 W
findings.value: an e-marked cable; without one, 3 A maximum (60 W at 20 V)
findings.source_title: Why is the Output Power of My Device Lower than 60W? (Anker support)
findings.note: Anker's words: 'To achieve output over 60W, an E-Marker cable must be used; without it, only 3A current is supported.' 3 A × 20 V = 60 W.

findings.label: Cable needed when a charger outputs more than 3 A
findings.value: 5 A cable with an E-Mark chip; with a 3 A e-marked cable the charger gives at most 20 V / 3 A
findings.note: Satechi's words: 'if the power adapter's electric current output is greater than 3A, a 5A wire with an E-Mark chip will be required.' Arithmetic: 65 W / 20 V = 3.25 A and 70 W / 20 V = 3.5 A, both above 3 A.
